passage:
Three weeks into guitar lessons in her Stockholm flat, Ulla threw the pick across the room. 'My fingers still buzz on the F chord. Mina, people online play this perfectly after a week.'
Mina, who had been playing for two years, didn't argue. Mina picked up Ulla's phone and found the first clip Ulla had recorded: day one, a shaky G chord and a nervous laugh.
'Listen to this,' Mina said, and played it. Then: 'Now play me the song you did yesterday.'
Ulla played it. Slow, a couple of buzzes, but the chords changed on time.
She was quiet for a moment. 'Okay. That's not the same person.'
'That's the only person you should be racing,' Mina said. They wrote a small goal on a sticky note: a clean F chord by the end of the month.

qa.q: What did Ulla record on day one?
qa.a: A shaky G chord and a nervous laugh.

qa.q: Why did Ulla throw the pick across the room?
qa.a: She felt frustrated that her fingers still buzzed on the F chord while people online seemed to play perfectly after a week.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ulla see her progress?
qa.a: Hearing her day-one clip next to yesterday's song showed how much she had improved, and they set one small goal: a clean F chord by month's end.

qa.q: How might Mina see Ulla's frustration, having played for two years?
qa.a: Mina probably understands it well and knows progress is slow, which is why Mina compared Ulla only with her own earlier self.

grounding: Shows a teenager impatient with slow progress who nearly gives up, until comparing with her own earlier self and setting small steps builds patience.

passage:
At the district sports club, Jahnavi slammed her locker. Two weeks of 6 a.m. running and her 800 metres time had dropped by just four seconds. 'It's useless. The girls in the senior group run under three minutes. I quit.'
Coach Shreya didn't try to talk her into staying. She opened the logbook. 'Your first day: you stopped twice. Walked the last bend. This morning?'
'I ran the whole way,' Jahnavi admitted.
'Four seconds is four seconds. And you didn't stop once. Try this: next Monday we mark one small thing, just one. Not the seniors. You against you.'
Jahnavi scuffed her shoe on the floor. 'One thing?'
'One thing.'
She shut the locker, softer this time. 'Fine. No stopping on the bend again.'

qa.q: By how much had Jahnavi's 800 metres time dropped?
What made Jahnavi want to quit?
qa.a: She felt her progress was useless because it was slow, and she was comparing herself with senior girls who run under three minutes.

qa.q: What choice did Coach Shreya make instead of pleading with Jahnavi to stay?
qa.a: She opened the logbook to compare Jahnavi with her own first day and suggested marking one small goal at a time.

qa.q: How might Coach Shreya see the four seconds differently from Jahnavi?
qa.a: Coach Shreya sees real progress, along with running the whole way, while Jahnavi sees only the gap to the seniors.

grounding: Shows a teenager who wants fast results in fitness and nearly quits, and how comparing with her own earlier self and small steps build patience.
